newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Trafalgar Square pigeons face cull.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Trafalgar Square pigeons face cull.

text.p: The pigeons of Trafalgar Square, stars of tourist snapshots the world over, are under threat.
With their droppings and sheer numbers threatening to engulf the area, the pigeons have come under the eagle eye of civil servants who consulted experts on what to do.
Suggestions have included bringing in trained hawks to frighten them off, planting wires and spikes in their roosting grounds, poisoning or even shooting them.
But the National Heritage Department which runs the square is acutely aware that tourists revel in the delights of feeding the birds for, as the song goes, "tuppence a bag."
"It is quite clear that the idea of a mass culling is ruled out," said a spokeswoman for the department on Tuesday after ministers were sent a consultation paper on the birds' fate.
She said authorities could "either discourage roosting in the square or how much they are fed there."
At present, the department grants a special licence to a vendor in the square who sells seed for feeding the pigeons.
"This keeps them in good condition. They are a healthy bunch," she said. "We try to discourage people feeding them sandwich leftovers or takeaways."
The Evening Standard newspaper had 10 London pigeons analysed by a British laboratory which found they harboured organisms that cause food poisoning, skin lesions and thrush.
The stomachs of the pigeons were found to contain Chinese food and hamburger wrappings.

Feeding the pigeons beneath the statue of Admiral Horatio Nelson ranks alongside the trooping of the colour at Buckingham Palace and a ride on a doubledecker red bus as a must for every visitor to the British capital.
In July, a British teenager provoked outrage and was fined 475 pounds ($700) for stealing pigeons from the square.
Police suspected they were destined for pigeon pies in local restaurants but Jason Lidbury, 18, said he was hoping to sell them to his uncle who kept racing pigeons.
The population at the height of the midsummer tourist season can top 1,000 but drop to less than 200 in the depths of winter.
But pigeon fanciers need not fear a mass slaughter, the spokeswoman said: "If we take action, it will be of a gentle sort. Can you imagine Trafalgar Square without the pigeons?"
